results.question: Describe a performance problem you solved.
results.answer: At Northwind Logistics I added read replicas and query indexes to our tracking API, and p95 latency went from 900 milliseconds to 180.

sentences.text: At Northwind Logistics, I was a Backend Engineer owning our shipment-tracking APIs built in Python and PostgreSQL.
Customers relied on us for real-time delivery tracking, but our p95 latency had crept up to 900 milliseconds and complaints were spiking during peak hours.

I dug into our slow query logs and database metrics, and I found two root causes: all that heavy read traffic was hitting our primary database, and our most common tracking lookups were missing indexes.
I put together a two-part plan to fix it: add read replicas to offload reads from the primary, and add targeted query indexes for our hottest endpoints.
I shipped the indexes first for a fast win, then carefully rolled out replica routing with testing to make sure we wouldn't introduce stale-read issues.
The impact was immediate — we brought p95 latency down from 900 milliseconds to 180 milliseconds.
That transformed the tracking experience for customers and drivers at peak, and it gave our primary database the headroom we needed to scale.

At Northwind Logistics, I was a backend engineer working on our shipment-tracking APIs in Python and Postgres.
We had a major incident where tracking went down for about three hours and customers couldn't get any shipment updates.
I joined the response and helped dig in, and we found a schema migration had taken a lock on our core shipments table.
That lock was blocking reads and writes, so traffic just piled up until everything timed out.
We stopped the migration, cleared the blocked queries, and brought the API back, then closely monitored latency and errors to confirm we were fully recovered.
Afterward, I owned writing the blameless postmortem.
I documented the timeline, the root cause, and why we hadn't caught the lock risk in review.
I also proposed guardrails going forward, like safer migration patterns, testing on production-like data, and clearer rollout and rollback steps.
It was a painful outage, but it made our team much more disciplined about database changes.

The most impactful thing I've built was re-architecting webhook delivery for the payments platform at Lumen Pay.
I was a Senior Backend Engineer on a team of six engineers, and reliable, real-time notifications were critical for our merchants.
When I joined the effort, we were running a cron poller that scanned the database every minute, which put our median delivery latency at around 40 seconds.
It got much worse during peak volume, and it was fragile and hard to scale.
I led the migration from that poller to an event-driven design on Kafka with dedicated delivery workers.
We added proper retry logic with exponential backoff and much better observability so we could see failures immediately.
That work cut our median delivery latency from 40 seconds down to 2 seconds.
It also eliminated the polling load on the database and made the system far more resilient during traffic spikes.
Merchants felt the difference right away, and it unlocked real-time use cases that just weren't possible before.
That's why I consider it my most impactful build, because it fundamentally changed how reliable and fast our platform felt to customers.
